claim: Human experience unfolds continuously in time but is not strictly linear, entailing cascading processes building hierarchical cognitive structures.
source: Even though human experience unfolds continuously in time, it is not strictly linear; instead, it entails cascading processes building hierarchical cognitive structures.
evidence: This is a general statement about human cognition presented in the abstract without specific experimental data or citations in this sentence.

claim: During speech perception, humans transform a continuously varying acoustic signal into phonemes, words, and meaning.
source: For instance, during speech perception, humans transform a continuously varying acoustic signal into phonemes, words, and meaning, and these levels all have distinct but interdependent temporal structures.
evidence: This is a well-established fact about speech perception presented as background knowledge.

claim: Phonemes, words, and meaning have distinct but interdependent temporal structures during speech perception.
source: For instance, during speech perception, humans transform a continuously varying acoustic signal into phonemes, words, and meaning, and these levels all have distinct but interdependent temporal structures.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the temporal organization of speech processing.

claim: Time-lagged regression using temporal response functions (TRFs) has emerged as a promising tool for disentangling electrophysiological brain responses related to complex models of perception.
source: Time-lagged regression using temporal response functions (TRFs) has recently emerged as a promising tool for disentangling electrophysiological brain responses related to such complex models of perception.
evidence: This is a general claim about the utility of TRFs, supported by the context of the paper and implied prior work.

claim: The Eelbrain Python toolkit makes TRF analysis easy and accessible.
source: Here, we introduce the Eelbrain Python toolkit, which makes this kind of analysis easy and accessible.
evidence: This is a claim about the toolkit being introduced in the paper, supported by the demonstration and examples provided throughout the manuscript.

claim: The Alice dataset contains EEG data from 33 participants who listened to the first chapter of Alice in Wonderland.
source: For this tutorial, we use the openly available Alice dataset (Bhattasali et al., 2020) which contains EEG data from 33 participants who listened to the first chapter of Alice in Wonderland (12.4 min; 2129 words).
evidence: This is a factual description of the dataset used, with a citation to the source.

claim: The first chapter of Alice in Wonderland used in the Alice dataset is 12.4 minutes long and contains 2129 words.
source: For this tutorial, we use the openly available Alice dataset (Bhattasali et al., 2020) which contains EEG data from 33 participants who listened to the first chapter of Alice in Wonderland (12.4 min; 2129 words).
evidence: This is a factual description of the stimulus properties.

claim: The Alice dataset includes several word-level regressors derived from different syntactic language models.
source: The dataset also includes several word-level regressors derived from different syntactic language models, described in more detail in the original publication (Brennan et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the contents of the dataset with a citation to the original publication.

claim: Eelbrain implements mTRF estimation using boosting.
source: Eelbrain implements mTRF estimation using boosting (David et al., 2007), as well as a variety of statistical tests, and ways to extract results for further analysis with other tools.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the implementation of the toolkit with a citation to the boosting algorithm.

claim: Boosting encourages TRFs with a small number of non-zero coefficients.
source: The choice of boosting is significant as it encourages TRFs with a small number of non-zero coefficients, i.e., the boosting algorithm prefers a simpler explanation over a complex one (Kulasingham and Simon, 2023).
evidence: This is a claim about the properties of the boosting algorithm, supported by a citation.

claim: Boosting is suitable for estimating mTRFs for models consisting of structured, highly correlated, and possibly redundant predictor variables.
source: This makes boosting suitable for estimating mTRFs for models consisting of structured, highly correlated, and possibly redundant predictor variables (David and Shamma, 2013), as is typical for models in cognitive neuroscience problems.
evidence: This is a claim about the suitability of boosting for certain types of problems, supported by a citation.

claim: The mTRF approach is built on the assumption that the brain response is continuously evolving in time as a function of the recently encountered stimulus.
source: The mTRF approach is built on the assumption that the brain response is continuously evolving in time as a function of the recently encountered stimulus (Lalor et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a fundamental assumption of the method, supported by a citation.

claim: Brain responses do not directly mirror a physical stimulus, but rather reflect a variety of transformations of that stimulus.
source: Brain responses do not directly mirror a physical stimulus, but rather reflect a variety of transformations of that stimulus.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about neural processing.

claim: Macroscopic cortical responses to speech are better described as responses to the slowly varying envelope of the original broadband signal rather than air pressure variations in the kHz range.
source: For example, while speech is transmitted through air pressure variations in the kHz range, this signal is transformed by the auditory periphery, and macroscopic cortical responses are better described as responses to the slowly varying envelope of the original broadband signal.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about auditory processing.

claim: In contrast to classical analysis approaches that require averaging, the convolution model applies to single trial data and does not require any repetition of identical stimuli.
source: In contrast to classical analysis approaches that require averaging, the convolution model applies to single trial data and does not require any repetition of identical stimuli.
evidence: This is a claim about the advantages of the convolution model compared to traditional approaches.

claim: The additive model of multiple predictor variables is consistent with the fact that macroscopic measurements of electrical brain signals reflect an additive superposition of signals from different brain regions.
source: This additive model is consistent with the fact that macroscopic measurements of electrical brain signals reflect an additive superposition of signals from different brain regions, potentially reflecting separable neural processes (Nunez and Srinivasan, 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to established knowledge about EEG signal properties.

claim: Predictor variables can be thought of as hypotheses about how stimuli are represented by the brain.
source: As such, predictor variables can be thought of as hypotheses about how stimuli are represented by the brain, and multiple concurrent predictors can embody distinct hypotheses about how the stimulus is transformed across different brain regions (Brodbeck and Simon, 2020).
evidence: This is a conceptual claim about the interpretation of predictor variables, supported by a citation.

claim: The additive nature of the convolution model allows it to be applied to comparatively natural stimulus conditions, such as audiobook listening.
source: The additive nature of the convolution model allows it to be applied to comparatively natural stimulus conditions, such as audiobook listening (Hamilton and Huth, 2020; Alday, 2019), while modeling natural variability through different predictor variables rather than minimizing it through experimental design.
evidence: This is a claim about the applicability of the method, supported by citations to examples.

claim: TRF analysis has yielded valuable insights into the way that perception and cognitive processes unfold over time.
source: This form of analysis has yielded valuable insights into the way that perception and cognitive processes unfold over time (e.g. Ding and Simon, 2012; Broderick et al., 2018; Brodbeck et al., 2018a; Daube et al., 2019; Liberto et al., 2021; Sohoglu and Davis, 2020).
evidence: This is a general claim about the utility of TRF analysis, supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: The auditory cortex is disproportionately sensitive to acoustic onsets.
source: For instance, it is known that the auditory cortex is disproportionately sensitive to acoustic onsets.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about auditory cortex function.

claim: Acoustic onset spectrograms are highly significant predictors of auditory magnetoencephalography (MEG) responses.
source: Indeed, such acoustic onset spectrograms are highly significant predictors of auditory magnetoencephalography (MEG) responses (Daube et al., 2019; Brodbeck et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a claim about the predictive power of acoustic onset spectrograms, supported by citations.

claim: A series of investigations suggests that brain responses to speech reflect linguistic representations at different hierarchical levels.
source: Furthermore, a series of such investigations suggests that brain responses to speech reflect linguistic representations at different hierarchical levels (Brodbeck et al., 2018a; Broderick et al., 2018; Weissbart et al., 2020; Gillis et al., 2021; Brodbeck et al., 2022).
evidence: This is a claim about hierarchical linguistic processing in the brain, supported by multiple citations.

claim: The power-law scale spectrogram was a better predictor of EEG data than the linear scale.
source: When considering the average predictive power at all electrodes, the power-law scale spectrogram was a better predictor than the linear scale (t(32) = 4.59, p<0.001)
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis presented in the paper.

claim: The log scale spectrogram improved predictions compared to the power-law scale.
source: and the log scale further improved predictions compared to the power-law scale (t(32) = 4.67, p<0.001).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the analysis presented in the paper.

claim: The linear + log combined model did not improve predictions over the logarithmic model.
source: The linear + log combined model did not improve predictions over the logarithmic model (Figure 3C), suggesting that the EEG responses to the acoustic power are sufficiently described by the logarithmic response scale and do not contain an additional linear component.
evidence: This is a finding from the analysis, supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: EEG responses to acoustic power are sufficiently described by the logarithmic response scale and do not contain an additional linear component.
source: The linear + log combined model did not improve predictions over the logarithmic model (Figure 3C), suggesting that the EEG responses to the acoustic power are sufficiently described by the logarithmic response scale and do not contain an additional linear component.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical comparison of models.

claim: Neural responses tend to scale logarithmically with acoustic power encoded in a spectrogram.
source: For instance, in the auditory system, neural responses tend to scale logarithmically with acoustic power encoded in a spectrogram (Rahman et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a claim about neural response properties, supported by a citation.

claim: The acoustic envelope alone is a very good predictor of held-out EEG responses, with variability explained reaching 82% of that of the full spectro-temporal model at anterior electrodes.
source: The envelope alone is already a very good predictor of held-out EEG responses, with variability explained reaching 82% of that of the full spectro-temporal model (Equation 3) at anterior electrodes.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the analysis presented in the paper.

claim: The TRF to the envelope exhibits features characteristic of auditory evoked responses to simple acoustic stimuli such as tones or isolated syllables, including a P1-N1-P2 sequence.
source: The TRF to the envelope exhibits features characteristic of auditory evoked responses to simple acoustic stimuli such as tones or isolated syllables, including a P1-N1-P2 sequence.
evidence: This is an observation from the TRF analysis, comparing it to known ERP components.

claim: Adding the one-dimensional acoustic onset predictor to the envelope model significantly improves the prediction of held-out responses compared to just the envelope (p<0.001).
source: Together, onset and envelope significantly improve the prediction of held-out responses compared to just the envelope (p<0.001), indicating that the onset representation is able to predict some aspects of the EEG responses that the envelope alone cannot.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the model comparison.

claim: The onset representation is able to predict some aspects of the EEG responses that the envelope alone cannot.
source: Together, onset and envelope significantly improve the prediction of held-out responses compared to just the envelope (p<0.001), indicating that the onset representation is able to predict some aspects of the EEG responses that the envelope alone cannot.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical finding of improved prediction.

claim: The typical TRF to acoustic onsets is of shorter duration than that to the envelope, and is characterized by two prominent peaks around 60 and 180 ms.
source: The typical TRF to the onsets is of shorter duration than that to the envelope, and is characterized by two prominent peaks around 60 and 180 ms.
evidence: This is a descriptive observation from the TRF analysis.

claim: While the acoustic envelope is a powerful predictor of EEG responses to speech, additional acoustic features can improve predictions further.
source: In sum, while the acoustic envelope is a powerful predictor of EEG responses to speech, additional acoustic features can improve predictions further, suggesting that they characterize neural representations that are not exhaustively described by the envelope.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion drawn from the analyses presented.

claim: Additional acoustic features beyond the envelope characterize neural representations that are not exhaustively described by the envelope.
source: In sum, while the acoustic envelope is a powerful predictor of EEG responses to speech, additional acoustic features can improve predictions further, suggesting that they characterize neural representations that are not exhaustively described by the envelope.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the improved predictive power of models with additional features.

claim: A significant response to acoustic onsets (after controlling for the envelope/spectrogram) provides evidence for a nonlinear component of the brain response to speech that represents acoustic onsets.
source: For instance, a significant response to acoustic onsets (after controlling for the envelope/spectrogram) provides evidence for a nonlinear component of the brain response to speech that represents acoustic onsets.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the interpretation of significant predictor contributions.

claim: Acoustic onsets might be especially important in segregating multiple auditory streams.
source: For example, acoustic onsets might be especially important in segregating multiple auditory streams (Brodbeck et al., 2020; Fiedler et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a claim about the functional role of acoustic onsets, supported by citations.

claim: The ERP contains stronger activity in the baseline period compared to the TRF.
source: A prominent difference is that the ERP contains stronger activity in the baseline period, and a larger deflection at late lags (starting at 600 ms), with a topography similar to acoustic activity (compare with Figure 4), indicating artifactual leakage from acoustic responses.
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison between ERP and TRF shown in Figure 5.

claim: The ERP shows artifactual leakage from acoustic responses at late lags (starting at 600 ms).
source: A prominent difference is that the ERP contains stronger activity in the baseline period, and a larger deflection at late lags (starting at 600 ms), with a topography similar to acoustic activity (compare with Figure 4), indicating artifactual leakage from acoustic responses.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed differences between ERP and TRF.

claim: The P2 peak in the TRF is temporally better defined (i.e. sharper) than in the ERPs.
source: Additionally, there is a significant difference at around 200–450 ms which could be attributed to the temporal spread of the observed P2 peak in the ERPs, as the P2 peak in the TRF is temporally better defined (i.e. sharper) than in the ERPs.
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison between ERP and TRF.

claim: The ERPs overestimate the responses to words.
source: Consistent with expectations, the ERPs overestimate the responses to words.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison between ERP and TRF analyses.

claim: The elevated baseline activity in ERPs suggests that the ERP is more prone to including brain activity that is not strictly a response to the stimulus feature.
source: The elevated baseline activity in particular suggests that the ERP is more prone to including brain activity that is not strictly a response to the stimulus feature, because the baseline period precedes the onset of the word.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the observed baseline differences.

claim: The TRF enables characterization of only the neural response time-locked to the particular feature of interest, while explicitly controlling for signal variability due to other features of the stimuli.
source: This highlights an advantage of the TRF paradigm over classical ERPs: the TRF enables characterization of only the neural response time-locked to the particular feature of interest, while explicitly controlling for signal variability due to other features of the stimuli.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the advantages of TRF analysis, supported by the comparison with ERPs.

claim: The predictive power of the model with the word class distinction (Equation 5) is significantly higher compared to the model without it (Equation 6) at a right anterior electrode cluster (p=0.002).
source: The predictive power of the model with the word class distinction (Equation 5) is significantly higher compared to the model without it (Equation 6) at a right anterior electrode cluster (p=0.002, Figure 6A, top).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the model comparison.

claim: Function words are associated with a larger positive response at anterior sensors than content words (when not controlling for acoustics).
source: This comparison suggests that function words are associated with a larger positive response at anterior sensors than content words.
evidence: This is an observation from the TRF comparison shown in Figure 6B.

claim: When controlling for acoustic features, the comparison of the predictive power of Equation 7 with Equation 4 no longer indicates a significant difference (p=0.065).
source: In contrast to the comparison without acoustics, the comparison of the predictive power of Equation 7 with Equation 4 no longer indicates a significant difference (p=0.065, Figure 6A, middle).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the model comparison.

claim: The information in the acoustic predictors can explain the difference between brain responses to function and content words in model Equation 5.
source: This suggests that the information in the acoustic predictors can explain the difference between brain responses to function and content words in model Equation 5.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the non-significant difference when controlling for acoustics.

claim: The model distinguishing function and content words is significantly better at predicting the spectrogram than the model treating all words equally (t(14) = 13.49, p<0.001).
source: With predictive power averaged across frequency bands, the model distinguishing function and content words is significantly better at predicting the spectrogram than the model treating all words equally (t(14) = 13.49, p<0.001), suggesting that function and content words indeed differ acoustically.
evidence: This is a statistical finding from the reverse analysis predicting spectrograms from word classes.

claim: Function and content words differ acoustically.
source: With predictive power averaged across frequency bands, the model distinguishing function and content words is significantly better at predicting the spectrogram than the model treating all words equally (t(14) = 13.49, p<0.001), suggesting that function and content words indeed differ acoustically.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical finding that word class predicts acoustic features.

claim: Function words, on average, have a sharper acoustic onset than content words.
source: Finally, the filter kernels to function and content words from this analysis can be interpreted as average acoustic patterns corresponding to the two word-classes (Figure 6C). This comparison suggests that function words, on average, have a sharper acoustic onset.
evidence: This is an observation from the acoustic analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: A reasonable explanation for the difference in neural responses by word class, when not controlling for acoustic features, is that it reflects sharper acoustic onsets of function words.
source: Since auditory cortex responses are known to be sensitive to acoustic onsets, a reasonable explanation for the difference in neural responses by word class, when not controlling for acoustic features, is that it reflects these sharper acoustic onsets of function words.
evidence: This is an inference combining the acoustic findings with known properties of auditory cortex.

claim: Model comparisons based on predictive power are generally more conservative than comparisons based on TRF estimates.
source: This has a good reason: model comparisons based on predictive power are generally more conservative than comparisons based on TRF estimates.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the relative conservativeness of different analysis approaches.

claim: TRFs are directly estimated on the training data, and are still prone to some overfitting.
source: First, TRFs are directly estimated on the training data, and are still prone to some overfitting (although the boosting algorithm aims to minimize that using the validation step and early stopping).
evidence: This is a methodological consideration about the properties of TRF estimation.

claim: If two predictors are correlated, they might share some of their predictive power.
source: Second, as in conventional regression models, if two predictors are correlated, that means that they might share some of their predictive power.
evidence: This is a general principle of regression analysis.

claim: mTRF estimates may always be contaminated by responses to correlated variables, especially when the correlations among predictor variables are high.
source: This means that mTRF estimates may always be contaminated by responses to correlated variables, especially when the correlations among predictor variables are high.
evidence: This is a methodological consideration about the interpretation of mTRFs.

claim: A significant result in a model comparison provides strong evidence that a given predictor contributes unique predictive power when compared to the other predictors included in the model.
source: In sum, a significant result in a model comparison provides strong evidence that a given predictor contributes unique predictive power when compared to the other predictors included in the model.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the interpretation of model comparisons.

claim: A significant effect in a TRF should always be interpreted with care, as it may also reflect the influence of other, correlated variables, even if those are included in the model.
source: In contrast, a significant effect in a TRF should always be interpreted with care, as it may also reflect the influence of other, correlated variables, even if those are included in the model.
evidence: This is a methodological caution about interpreting TRF results.

claim: The sparsity prior in the boosting algorithm will favor a model with smaller coefficients.
source: In contrast to this, a sparsity prior will favor a model with smaller coefficients.
evidence: This is a property of the sparsity prior used in boosting.

claim: An uncentered predictor that can explain responses with a small coefficient in the intercept term will be preferable over a centered predictor that requires a larger intercept coefficient (under a sparsity prior).
source: Consequently, an uncentered predictor that can explain responses with a small coefficient in the intercept term will be preferable over a centered predictor that requires a larger intercept coefficient.
evidence: This is a consequence of the sparsity prior's preference for smaller coefficients.

claim: Sometimes mathematically redundant predictors can improve the predictive power of a model under a sparsity prior.
source: Another consequence of the same preference for sparser models is that sometimes mathematically redundant predictors can improve the predictive power of a model.
evidence: This is a consequence of the sparsity prior in boosting.

claim: When data is recorded from a dense enough sensor array, neural source localization can be used to estimate a reconstruction of the sources contributing to the mixture signal, and assign the different brain responses to their cortical locations.
source: When data is recorded from a dense enough sensor array, neural source localization can be used to estimate a reconstruction of the sources contributing to the mixture signal, and assign the different brain responses to their cortical locations (Nunez and Srinivasan, 2006).
evidence: This is a claim about source localization methods, supported by a citation.

claim: Source localization can improve the signal-to-noise ratio of a specific response, because it acts as a spatial filter.
source: In many cases, source localization can also improve the signal-to-noise ratio of a specific response, because it acts as a spatial filter, aggregating information that is relevant for a given brain region across sensors, and suppressing signals whose likely origin is a different location.
evidence: This is a claim about the benefits of source localization.

claim: The choice of referencing strategy has minimal influence on the magnitude of the prediction accuracies averaged across channels or the latencies of the TRF peaks.
source: Although the reference has minimal influence on the magnitude of the prediction accuracies averaged across channels or the latencies of the TRF peaks, it does have a substantial impact on the distribution across the EEG channels (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison of different referencing strategies shown in Figure 7.

claim: The choice of referencing strategy has a substantial impact on the distribution of predictive power across the EEG channels.
source: Although the reference has minimal influence on the magnitude of the prediction accuracies averaged across channels or the latencies of the TRF peaks, it does have a substantial impact on the distribution across the EEG channels (Figure 7).
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison shown in Figure 7.

claim: TRF analysis has been successfully applied to music perception.
source: While cortical processing of speech has been a primary application for mTRF analysis, the technique has potential applications in any domain where stimuli unfold in time, and has already been successfully applied to music perception (Liberto et al., 2021; Leahy et al., 2021)
evidence: This is a claim about applications of TRF analysis, supported by citations.

claim: TRF analysis has been successfully applied to audiovisual speech perception.
source: and has already been successfully applied to music perception (Liberto et al., 2021; Leahy et al., 2021), audiovisual speech perception (Crosse et al., 2016b)
evidence: This is a claim about applications of TRF analysis, supported by a citation.

claim: TRF analysis has been successfully applied to subcortical auditory processing.
source: and has already been successfully applied to music perception (Liberto et al., 2021; Leahy et al., 2021), audiovisual speech perception (Crosse et al., 2016b), and subcortical auditory processing (Maddox and Lee, 2018).
evidence: This is a claim about applications of TRF analysis, supported by a citation.

claim: In multi-talker speech, TRFs to speech features change as a function of whether the listener attends to the given speech stream or not.
source: For example, in multi-talker speech, TRFs to speech features change as a function of whether the listener attends to the given speech stream or not (Ding and Simon, 2012; Brodbeck et al., 2018a; Broderick et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a claim about attention-dependent TRF changes, supported by citations.

claim: TRF analysis allows for determining whether a given feature makes a unique contribution over and beyond other features of the same stimulus.
source: In addition, analysis of the prediction accuracy allows for determining whether a given feature makes a unique contribution over and beyond other features of the same stimulus.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the capabilities of TRF analysis.

claim: Using cross-validation, models are assessed based on their predictive power, not just their explanatory power, thus providing an overall stronger test than conventional models.
source: Finally, using cross-validation, models are assessed based on their predictive power, not just their explanatory power, thus providing an overall stronger test than conventional models.
evidence: This is a methodological claim about the advantages of cross-validation in TRF analysis.

claim: Major cortical phase-locked responses decrease quickly above 10 Hz.
source: The major cortical phase-locked responses decrease quickly above 10 Hz (Ding et al., 2014), although there can be exceptions, such as a pitch-following response up to 100 Hz (Kulasingham et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a claim about the frequency characteristics of cortical responses, supported by citations.

claim: A 50 ms Hamming window basis leads to significantly better predictive power than the default impulse basis.
source: In this case, a 50 ms Hamming window basis leads to significantly better predictive power than the default impulse basis (Figure 10A).
evidence: This is a finding from the comparison of different basis functions shown in Figure 10.

claim: Using a wider basis window leads to markedly smoother TRFs, and increases the overlap of the TRFs between subjects.
source: Figure 10C shows that using a wider basis window leads to markedly smoother TRFs, and increases the overlap of the TRFs between subjects.
evidence: This is an observation from the comparison shown in Figure 10C.

claim: Boosting mTRF captures the dominant features of the ground truth mTRF.
source: Both the mTRFs recovered by boosting and ridge regression capture the dominant features of the ground truth mTRF.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation study shown in Figure 9.

claim: The boosting mTRF has only a few peaks and troughs, giving a simpler representation with peaks and troughs closely corresponding to those of the ground truth.
source: However, the boosting mTRF has only a few peaks and troughs, giving a simpler representation with peaks and troughs closely corresponding to those of the ground truth, while the ridge regression mTRF includes many additional noisy peaks and troughs (Figure 9A, middle, and right panel; see also David et al., 2007; David and Shamma, 2013).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation study, supported by references to prior work.

claim: The ridge regression mTRF includes many additional noisy peaks and troughs compared to the boosting mTRF.
source: However, the boosting mTRF has only a few peaks and troughs, giving a simpler representation with peaks and troughs closely corresponding to those of the ground truth, while the ridge regression mTRF includes many additional noisy peaks and troughs (Figure 9A, middle, and right panel; see also David et al., 2007; David and Shamma, 2013).
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation study shown in Figure 9.

claim: Ridge regression follows the dominant peaks and troughs of the ground truth mTRF closely, but acquires numerous false positives.
source: The ridge regression follows the dominant peaks and troughs of the ground truth mTRF closely, but, in doing so, acquires numerous false positives, i.e., small non-zero values when the true mTRF is actually zero.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation study shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The boosting mTRF displays a high true negative rate, while biasing the peaks and troughs towards zero.
source: On the other hand, the boosting mTRF displays a high true negative rate, while biasing the peaks and troughs towards zero.
evidence: This is an observation from the simulation study shown in Figure 9B.

claim: The average interval between word onsets in the Alice stimulus set is 334 ms.
source: This is not surprising considering that the ERP is just an average of neural signals before and after word onsets, which includes, besides the responses to the words, neural responses to the acoustic signal, as well as activities that are not time-locked (including overlapping responses to the previous and next word, given that the average interval between word onsets in this stimulus set is only 334 ms).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the stimulus properties.
